I am, yes. Fabio Segura, from Bradesco. I am based in Sao Paulo.
Good to meet you. Which part of the bank are you in? It is a big place.
The wholesale banking side. I oversee innovation for a division that handles foreign exchange, trade services and trade finance.
Right. And what is on your desk this year? I am asking because half this floor sells the same thing.
Two things. We are replacing a settlement platform that is older than my team, and we are running a pilot on stablecoins. Both of them are about cross-border payments.
Now we are talking. How long does a remittance take today, on your side?
Two days to Europe, sometimes three. My clients ask me why, and I do not have a good answer yet. What does Northgate actually do — are you the rails, or the layer on top?

Note to the team, end of day one on the exhibition floor. I spoke to people from about thirty banks today, and I want to write down the pattern while it is fresh. The ones I remember are not the ones with the best English. They are the ones who told me three things in the first ninety seconds. What part of the bank they sit in. What they are working on right now, this year, not in general. And what they came here to find. That is all. When somebody gives me those three, I already know whether to book a meeting. When somebody gives me a job title and then waits for me to ask questions, the conversation dies in front of the stand, and we both pretend it was the noise.

People ask me what we listen for when a bank walks up to the stand, and the honest answer is that we listen for the difference between a description and a problem. Anyone can describe a bank. Wholesale division, trade finance, cross-border payments, five hundred people. Fine. That tells me nothing I could not read on your website. What I am listening for is the sentence after that. We are replacing a settlement platform this year. We are running a pilot on stablecoins. Our remittance flow takes two days and our clients are asking why. The moment somebody says a sentence in the present continuous, I know they are inside a real project, and I start taking notes. Until then, I am just being polite.

Cross-border payments move around one hundred and fifty trillion dollars a year, and for most of the last fifty years that money has travelled through a chain of correspondent banks, each one adding a day and a fee. That is the problem the industry meets to solve every autumn at Sibos, the conference the Swift network has been running since the nineteen seventies. What has changed recently is who is in the room. Ten years ago the exhibition floor was banks and card networks. Now it is banks, card networks, stablecoin issuers and a long line of infrastructure companies that did not exist when the last system was built. And this is why the introduction matters more than it used to. A director of innovation at a large bank is not walking that floor to learn what a payment is. She is walking it to find the three companies, out of four hundred, that are already solving the exact problem her team is working on this quarter.
